Final AI Project — Fundación Mexicana del Corazón

Eduardo Casarrubias Solano · MGT 409 AI Foundations for Managers · Yale SOM · October 2026

Live app (use this first): https://fmc-heart-campaign-3d.onrender.com · management dashboard: https://fmc-heart-campaign-3d.onrender.com/#/staff

GitHub repo (to clone): https://github.com/eduardohub555/fmc-heart-campaign-3d

The live app and a fresh clone both open with the same demo data: 50 fictional donors (12 companies), their donations, receipts, thank-you emails and conversations. To manage, choose Sign up at /#/staff (name, email, password). The free server sleeps when idle, so the first visit can take about a minute.

What it does. This app lets potential donors learn about heart disease and create an account to make one-time or recurring donations. It also helps the management team of Fundación Mexicana del Corazón track donations and distribute them to patients who need heart surgery.

1. Motivation

Three years ago I was diagnosed with dysautonomia, a condition that can make me faint under stress, sleep deprivation or dehydration. I was lucky to have a job and be able to afford my medication. Then I learned that about 1 in every 4 deaths in Mexico is caused by heart disease: INEGI's 2024 death statistics record roughly 190,000 heart-disease deaths out of about 820,000. I felt I needed to do something. My doctor introduced me to Fundación Mexicana del Corazón.

The idea is a campaign for people who need heart surgery and cannot afford it. We estimate about 200,000 MXN per surgery, everything included. The Instituto Nacional de Cardiología (INC) performs the surgeries, and the foundation raises the money. All of us have a sister, a friend or a coworker who may face one of these conditions. The goal is to give the foundation a way to motivate people to learn about heart health, and then, only if their wallet allows, to donate.

2. What is new here

  • Interactive and emotional instead of a donation form. Most donation pages are a form and a button. Here you walk through the INC gardens and meet eight characters: four professionals and four family members. Mateo (9) tells you his little sister Valentina has "a tiny hole in her heart" and he just wants to play soccer with her again. Don Ernesto thought his heart attack was heartburn from too many tacos. Doña Rosa's valve was damaged by untreated throat infections in childhood. When a child can't answer a medical question, he sends you to the doctor, and the doctor already knows what you two talked about (Figures 3–4).
  • Education first, grounded in sources. Agent #1 (the Teacher) may only use a curated knowledge base from trusted sources: WHO, INEGI, the American Heart Association, the U.S. NIH and the INC. It never invents facts and never pushes anyone to donate. Every conversation ends with a specific, sourced health reminder, such as heart-attack warning signs, salt below 5 g a day, or 7–9 hours of sleep.
  • Tax receipts built in. Most foundations treat the deductible receipt as a separate, manual process. Here donors enter their tax ID (RFC) once, either personal or their company's. Each thank-you email then comes with a receipt that has a folio and that RFC. This saves donors time, and could make companies prefer us because the tax savings are easier to claim.
  • A live management dashboard. Totals, charts, the donor table, the surgery payments and the agents' work are all in one screen. I don't have enough experience with foundations' internal tools to claim how new this part is, but it removes a lot of spreadsheet work (see Impact).

3. The agents

The app has four agents built with PydanticAI. All four use one model, gpt-6-luna, through Portkey, with reasoning turned off. I chose it because it is the course's model and the cheapest available: US$0.10 per 1M input tokens and US$0.50 per 1M output, which is 100× cheaper than gpt-6-astra. It is also fast (2–4 seconds per answer), and every task here is short and well defined. Anything that must be exact (money, counts, dates, receipts) is done in code, not by a model.

Figure 2. How the agents communicate. Blue arrows happen on every run. The dashed orange link (#3 → #2) is only used when the Coordinator finds the Accountant's figures inconsistent.

AgentWhat it doesTools it uses (all code; no web access)
#1 TeacherAnswers visitors in the voice of each doctor, social worker, child, parent or grandparent. It replies in English or Spanish, refers visitors to the right character, and sends a Q&A report to #2 when a chat ends.Curated knowledge base; each character's story; the conversation passed on from the referring character; a source-ID validator that drops any invented source; pre-written closing health tips.
#2 AccountantRecords donations and surgery payments, issues receipts with the RFC, and computes the budget and the "topics vs. donations" table. A model is used only for the plain-language management summary.SQL ledger; budget and reconciliation functions; receipt issuer; RFC validator. Every figure comes from donors' and managers' records.
#3 CoordinatorReads #2's table, the questions the Teacher couldn't answer, and recent letters. It sends guidance to #1 and #4, and a list of knowledge gaps for staff to research. It also checks #2's figures and writes to #2 only if something doesn't match.Correlation table; list of unanswered questions and reported errors; ledger reconciliation; "every number must exist in the table" checker.
#4 WriterDrafts bilingual thank-you emails from the patient to the donor, in the patient's own voice (a 6-year-old writes like a child). One-time donors are invited to give again; monthly donors are thanked for their constant support. It translates managers' edits into the other language, and never sends anything.Patient record; deterministic receipt note with the exact RFC; placeholder blocker; "constant support" check that triggers a re-draft.

4. Tokenomics

Every model call is logged with its input, cached-input and output tokens and its cost (Figure 14). Prices for gpt-6-luna: US$0.10 per 1M input, US$0.01 per 1M cached input, US$0.50 per 1M output. The numbers below come from the real run in Section 3.

Coordinator round (guidance + #1 and #4 replies)3,23607020.00068

One typical run: a visitor asks 3 questions, uses 9,455 input tokens (5,238 cached) and 459 output, and costs US$0.0007. If they donate, the bilingual email adds US$0.00024, for a total of about US$0.001 per donor. The closing card, health tips, stories, receipts, budget and reconciliation cost nothing, because they are pre-written or computed in code.

Per user per month (one visit with 3 questions, and a monthly letter for 30% of users): about US$0.0008. Managing the campaign (4 Accountant summaries and 4 Coordinator rounds a month) adds US$0.004 a month in total.

Hosting is separate. The demo runs on Render's free plan; a production version needs a paid plan and a lasting database. For reference, the whole development and testing effort (295 model calls, including 50 simulated visitors and 100+ letters) cost about US$0.07.

How we kept the cost down

  • Work split across agents and code. The model is used only where language is needed. Numbers, receipts, tips, stories and procedure explanations are code or pre-written text.
  • Prompt caching. The Teacher's fixed instructions and knowledge base come first in the prompt, so repeated questions are served 83% from cache. That cut the cost per answer from US$0.00038 to US$0.00016, and the cost of a 3-question visit by 40%.
  • Small, capped calls. Reasoning is off. Answers are capped at about 120 words (450 output tokens). Only the last 3 exchanges are re-sent. Every run has a token ceiling and a timeout.
  • Fewer calls. The Accountant's model is only used when a manager asks for a summary. #3 contacts #2 only when figures don't match, and the Writer re-drafts only when a monthly letter misses "constant support".

Did cost cutting hurt quality?

Once, yes, and the tests caught it. To save tokens, the Teacher first received only each character's personality, not their story. In the 50-visitor test, Mariana said she didn't know how they found out Luis was sick, and Don Ernesto couldn't describe his own heart attack. Adding the story (about 100 tokens) fixed it. Two trade-offs remain. Short answers sometimes leave a follow-up question for the visitor. And sending only the last 3 exchanges means a very long conversation can lose early details, although a referral passes the relevant context on to the next character.

5. Safety

  • Passwords and sessions. Donor and manager passwords are stored only as salted scrypt hashes. Session tokens are random and stored only as a SHA-256 hash. Secrets live in .env, which is never committed (the repo has .env.example only).
  • Prompt injection and data leaks. The agents never see donor records, so there is nothing for them to leak. The honesty rules are in every prompt: never lie or invent data, never pressure, teach rather than maximize donations, and no personal medical advice (call 911 for emergencies). Figure 15 shows an attack being refused. The provider's own content filter is a second layer; when it blocks a prompt, the visitor gets a polite reply in their language.
  • Agent malfunction. Invented facts are limited because only the knowledge base can be used and unknown source IDs are dropped. Wrong numbers can't reach managers because #2's figures are computed in code and #3 checks them against the ledger (Figure 16). Wrong actions are limited because agents can't send email, move money or change records: managers do that, and a sent email is locked. Infinite loops are prevented by a request limit and a timeout on every run.
  • Overspending. Every run has a token ceiling. Messages are capped at 600 characters and visits at 40 questions. The tokenomics dashboard makes spending visible, and the Portkey key can carry its own budget limit. Managers can't record payments larger than the money available.

6. Impact

There is no counterfactual for money raised yet, so here is a careful estimate of the time saved and what the money can do. These are estimates, not measurements, and every assumption is stated.

WhoWithout the app (assumption)With the appTime saved
Donor wanting a deductible receiptEmail RFC and fiscal data, follow up: ~10 min per donationRFC entered once; receipt arrives with the thank-you: ~1 min~9 min per donation; ~1.8 h a year per monthly donor
Management, per donationRecord in a spreadsheet 3 min, receipt 5 min, letter 10 min, translation 5 min: ~23 minReview and send the drafted bilingual email: ~2 min~21 min
Management, monthly reportReconcile, build charts and a summary: ~4 hLive dashboard, #2 summary, #3 check: ~0.5 h~3.5 h

At the demo's volume of 50 donations a month, management saves about 21 hours a month (about 2.6 working days), and donors who want receipts save about 6 hours together (41 of 50 gave an RFC). That time can go to patients and fundraising.

People helped. At about 200,000 MXN per surgery, the 50 demo donors (MXN 2,141,000) would fund about 10 surgeries, and the demo's monthly donors add MXN 38,600 a month, or about 2.3 more surgeries a year. A more modest real scenario: if 1,000 visitors come, 10% give 1,000 MXN once, and 20 give 1,000 MXN a month, that's MXN 340,000 in a year, or about 1.7 surgeries. These figures use the campaign estimate, not INC prices.

The most important impact is education. Every visitor leaves knowing at least one sourced, practical habit: the warning signs of a heart attack and to call 911, salt below 5 g a day, 150 minutes of activity a week, 7–9 hours of sleep, or treating strep throat in children. They hear these through patients' stories. With heart disease causing 1 in 4 deaths in Mexico, a visitor who learns to recognize a heart attack or to check their blood pressure may help themselves or someone close. Donating stays optional.

7. Limits and next steps

  1. Real patients, with consent. The five patients and their families are fictional. A real version needs INC patient data, with privacy safeguards and consent for stories and letters.
  2. Restrict manager accounts. For the professor and TAs, anyone can sign up as a manager with an email and password. Before real use, only invited foundation staff should get access, with roles and two-factor authentication.
  3. Official tax receipts. Today's receipts are prototypes. Issuing real CFDIs means meeting SAT's requirements: a stamping provider (PAC), the foundation's RFC and fiscal data, and the donor's fiscal regime and address.
  4. Real emails and payments. Thank-you emails should actually be sent (with the donor's opt-in), and a payment provider should be connected so real money flows in, for cards, transfers and recurring charges.
  5. Transfers to the hospital. Bank transfers from the foundation to the INC per patient, so a recorded payment becomes a scheduled surgery, with confirmation back to the donor.
  6. Harden for scale. A lasting database instead of the free plan's temporary disk, rate limits per IP address, and a budget cap on the API key. A doctor at the INC should also review the knowledge base, and the gaps the Coordinator flags should be filled from trusted sources.

Built with React, three.js, FastAPI, PydanticAI and gpt-6-luna via Portkey. All code: https://github.com/eduardohub555/fmc-heart-campaign-3d · Live: https://fmc-heart-campaign-3d.onrender.com
